methods.title: Engineering stress-strain from a tensile test
methods.when: The metals and polymers tensile labs: force and displacement from the test frame, reduced to material properties.
steps: Measure the gauge length, width, and thickness before the test (and after it, for reduction in area). Compute the original area A0 = width x thickness.
Engineering stress = force / A0. Engineering strain = elongation / original gauge length. Build both as formula columns.
Plot stress (vertical) against strain (horizontal) with markers for the measured points.
Modulus of elasticity: the slope of a line fitted over the clearly linear initial region. State which points were used.
Yield strength by the 0.2% offset: draw a line with the elastic slope shifted by a strain of 0.002 and read the stress where it crosses the curve.
Tensile strength: the maximum engineering stress.
Ductility: percent elongation = (final length - original length) / original length x 100, and percent reduction in area from the before and after areas when they were measured.
Resilience: the area under the elastic portion (about yield stress squared over twice the modulus). Toughness: the area under the whole curve to fracture, by the trapezoid rule over every data row.
Compare each property with a handbook or textbook value for the same material and condition, cite where it came from, and explain any difference.
pitfalls: Reporting the peak force in lbf as the tensile strength.
Resilience and toughness formulas covering the same row range. Toughness has to run to the fracture row. When the two come out equal, the range is wrong.
A modulus well below the handbook value, because crosshead displacement includes machine and grip compliance. Say so rather than adjusting the data.
Comparing against a reference value for a different alloy, temper, or cold-work state, or leaving the reference column blank for one of the two materials.
Formula references hard-coded to one sample's rows and then copied to the other sample's table without being updated.

methods.title: Relaxation modulus from a held-strain test
methods.when: The polymers lab: the crosshead is paused in the plastic region and the force is read each second as it decays.
steps: Record the held strain once, and the force every second from the test video.
Stress at each time = force / A0, using the original area as for engineering stress.
Relaxation modulus Er(t) = stress(t) / held strain. Tabulate it against time and plot it.
Report Er at the time the handout names. When it names none, state the time you chose; the textbook convention is 10 s.
Contrast with creep: relaxation holds strain and watches stress fall, while creep holds load and watches strain grow.
pitfalls: Reporting a list of moduli with no time attached.
Taking the strain from a moment when the elongation was still rising, because the video shows it creeping for a few seconds after the pause.

methods.title: Compressive strength and acceptance statistics for concrete cylinders
methods.when: The concrete 2 lab: fracture forces from the class's cylinders, a supplier's 7-day and 28-day record, and historical class data.
steps: Compressive strength = fracture force / (pi x diameter^2 / 4). Confirm the cylinder diameter for every data set before computing.
Tabulate the count, minimum, maximum, mean, and standard deviation for each group the sheet asks about (7-day, 28-day, with and without entrained air).

Plot what the hand-in list names: a bar chart of 7-day against 28-day strength, histograms of the historical strengths (with and without air, as separate figures), and scatter plots of strength against water/cement ratio and against percent air.

Judge acceptance against the standard the course links on Moodle, which was not retained. ACI 318 is the usual basis (a running average of three consecutive tests and a floor on any single test), but use the course's document when the student has it.
Compare each trend with the expected direction (strength falls as water/cement ratio rises and as air content rises), and explain any scatter from mix or testing differences.
pitfalls: The historical data and the class's own cylinders may not share a cylinder size, so one area formula applied to both is wrong for one of them.
Air content entered as a fraction in some rows and as a percent in others. Check the column before plotting it.
Calling a mix acceptable from its mean alone without checking the individual-test criterion.

assignment_families.title: Lab report sheet with workbook (polymers, concrete 2)
stages: read the posted lab procedure and answer the preparation questions
attend the scheduled test (group or individual, per the handout) and record data in the sheet's table
reduce the data in Excel, either in the instructor's workbook or one built to the same structure
answer every question in place and insert each requested table and figure
upload the workbook and hand in or upload the completed sheet
deliverables: the completed report sheet (Word, or printed and stapled where the handout says so)
the Excel workbook as a separate upload
what_good_looks_like: Every numbered question is answered directly under it, and none is left blank.
Every item on the hand-in list appears as a numbered, captioned figure or table with units, inserted into the sheet and not printed from Excel.
Each derived property states its value, its units, and one sentence on how it was determined.
The workbook computes every reported number with formulas, and the report matches it exactly.
Trend and acceptance questions are answered with the relevant statistic or criterion named, not just yes or no.
assignment_families.basis: two report-sheet handouts (polymers, concrete 2), one completed polymers sheet, the concrete workbook. No graded return exists.

assignment_families.title: Short tensile-test write-up (metals)
stages: write a short report with a property table and figures
deliverables: a short Word report with a title block, a method summary, a property table, a discussion, and an appendix of stress-strain figures
what_good_looks_like: The property table gives each property's value with units, how it was found, and a cited reference value for the same material and condition.
The discussion explains each large difference from the reference with a physical or procedural reason.
The stress-strain figures are numbered, captioned, and have labeled axes with units.

assignment_families.title: Societal and environmental issues presentation
stages: read the assigned textbook chapter and complete its activities
claim a material from the approved list
research it against the handout's topic list
deliverables: a recorded presentation of about 6-10 slides with the presenter's voice, uploaded to Moodle
what_good_looks_like: Every topic on the handout's list is covered, because the list is also the grading rubric: what the material is and its molecular structure with a diagram, the full materials cycle through end of life, its purpose, its costs and who bears them, and a Christian-perspective evaluation using the design norms.
Slides use images and short bullets, not paragraphs.
Sources appear on each slide or on a closing references slide, and they are judged for quality (the handout names the CRAAP test).
The narration shows command of the material rather than reading the slides.

magnitudes.quantity: held strain in the polymer stress-relaxation test (engineering strain, as a fraction)
magnitudes.basis: Physical plausibility, not a course rule: the hold is in the plastic region of a thermoplastic tensile test, where engineering strain is a small fraction up to a few times the gauge length.
magnitudes.note: Between about 3 and 300: strain entered as a percent. Every relaxation modulus built on it comes out 100x low.

magnitudes.quantity: relaxation modulus Er at about 10 s (thermoplastic at room temperature)
magnitudes.basis: Physical plausibility, not a course rule: room-temperature thermoplastics sit roughly between a few tens of MPa (soft polyethylene, well into yield) and a few GPa (glassy polymers). Textbook property tables.
magnitudes.note: About 100x low: the held strain went in as a percent. About 1000x off: stress in Pa or kPa labelled MPa. If the specimen is an elastomer, not a thermoplastic, 1-20 MPa is normal and this range does not apply. 1 MPa = 145 psi.

magnitudes.quantity: tensile strength of a metal lab specimen (steel, aluminum, brass)
magnitudes.basis: Physical plausibility, not a course rule: common engineering alloys have ultimate strengths from about 10 ksi (annealed pure aluminum) to about 200 ksi (hardened steel). Handbook values.
magnitudes.note: Equal to the peak force, or below about 10,000: the peak force was reported without dividing by the original area. A lab specimen's area is well under 1 in^2, so the strength is always numerically larger than the force in lbf.

magnitudes.quantity: modulus of elasticity of a metal from the tensile test
magnitudes.basis: Physical plausibility, not a course rule: handbook moduli are about 10,000 ksi for aluminum, 15,000 for brass and 29,000 for steel. Crosshead displacement includes grip and machine compliance, so a measured modulus well below handbook is expected and is why the low bound is generous.
magnitudes.note: Above the handbook value for the alloy: something is wrong, since compliance can only lower it. About 100x low: strain as a percent. About 1000x off: psi and ksi confused.

magnitudes.basis: Physical plausibility, not a course rule: ductile wrought alloys elongate roughly 10-60% and cast or hardened ones a few percent. Handbook values.
magnitudes.note: Below 1 for a visibly ductile specimen: reported as a fraction, not a percent. Above 100: lengths in different units, or the fraction multiplied by 100 twice.

magnitudes.quantity: ratio of toughness to resilience (same specimen)
magnitudes.basis: Physical plausibility, not a course rule: resilience is only the elastic triangle, while toughness integrates the whole curve to fracture, so for any metal that yields before breaking toughness is many times larger.
magnitudes.note: About 1: the toughness integral stopped at the same row as the resilience range. It has to run to the fracture row.

magnitudes.quantity: compressive strength of a concrete cylinder
magnitudes.basis: Handout and physical plausibility: the concrete report sheet frames acceptance against required strengths of 3,000 to 4,000 psi, and ordinary concrete breaks between about 2,000 and 8,000 psi. The bounds are a generous plausibility margin around both, not a course rule.
magnitudes.note: About 4x low: the radius was used as the diameter in pi d^2/4. About 2.25x off: a 4 in cylinder's area applied to a 6 in cylinder, or the reverse. The report sheet itself names both sizes in different parts, so check the diameter for every data set. Acceptance is judged per cylinder against the required strength, not from the mean.

magnitudes.quantity: ratio of 7-day to 28-day compressive strength (same mix)
magnitudes.basis: Physical plausibility, not a course rule: concrete gains strength as it cures, and a 7-day cylinder usually reaches roughly two-thirds to three-quarters of its 28-day strength.
magnitudes.note: Above 1: the columns are swapped, or the groups used different cylinder sizes. A single odd pair can be real scatter; a whole data set above 1 is not.

magnitudes.basis: Physical plausibility, not a course rule: entrapped air in plain concrete is a percent or two, and air-entrained mixes run about 4-8%.
magnitudes.note: Below 0.5 in a column that is otherwise percent: those rows were entered as fractions. Check the column before plotting strength against it.

magnitudes.basis: Physical plausibility, not a course rule: workable structural mixes fall roughly between 0.35 and 0.7 by mass.
magnitudes.note: Above 1 or near 30-80: entered as a percent, or the ratio inverted to cement/water.
